subject: Accounting
title: Posting: Connecting Journal to Ledger
description: A quick win: understand Posting: Connecting Journal to Ledger.

hook.text: You wrote the journal entry. Now it needs to reach the ledger. That transfer is called posting.

buildup.text: Posting moves each debit and credit from the journal entry into the appropriate ledger account.

discovery.text: Reference numbers link each ledger entry back to its original journal entry—creating an audit trail.

twist.text: Modern software posts instantly. Manually, bookkeepers once spent hours posting entries each day.

climax.text: Posting is the bridge between recording a transaction and seeing its effect on account balances.

punchline.text: Journal captures it. Posting places it. Ledger keeps it.

quiz.question: What is posting in bookkeeping?
options: Transferring journal entries to the ledger

details.summary: Posting is the process of transferring journal entry information to individual accounts in the general ledger. This topic explains how posting connects day-to-day transaction recording to the organized account structure that produces financial statements.
details.whyItMatters: Without posting, journal entries remain a chronological list with no way to see running balances for individual accounts. Posting organizes data so you can quickly check any account's current balance.
takeaways: Posting transfers debits and credits from the journal to their respective ledger accounts
Each posted entry includes the date, amount, and a reference back to the original journal entry
Modern software posts automatically, but understanding the process helps catch errors

faq.question: What is posting in bookkeeping?
faq.answer: Posting is transferring each debit and credit from a journal entry to the appropriate account in the general ledger. This transforms a chronological transaction record into organized account-by-account records showing running balances.

faq.question: Is posting still done manually?
faq.answer: Accounting software handles posting automatically when transactions are recorded. However, understanding the posting process is essential for comprehending how financial data flows from transactions to trial balances to financial statements, and for troubleshooting errors.
